result.summary: Apollodorus traces the descendants of the Pleiades, including Hermes' theft of Apollo's cattle and the Spartan royal line. It ends with the birth of Helen and the suitors' oath sworn to Tyndareus.

scenes.title: The Pleiades and their children
scenes.summary: Atlas and Pleione's seven daughters are listed, with the children of Poseidon and Zeus.

scenes.title: Hermes steals Apollo's cattle
scenes.summary: Newborn Hermes steals Apollo's cattle, invents the lyre, and is found out. He trades the lyre and pipe to Apollo for the cattle, the wand and divination.
scenes.stakes: Hermes risks punishment by Zeus for the theft.

scenes.title: Lacedaemon's line and Aesculapius
scenes.summary: The descendants of Taygete are traced down through Sparta's kings. Apollo's son Aesculapius becomes a healer who raises the dead.

scenes.title: Zeus punishes Aesculapius and Apollo
scenes.summary: Zeus kills Aesculapius with a thunderbolt. Apollo kills the Cyclopes and serves Admetus for a year.
scenes.stakes: Apollo faces being hurled into Tartarus.

scenes.title: Hippocoon, Leda and Helen
scenes.summary: Hippocoon expels Tyndareus and Icarius, who return after Hercules kills him. Helen is born to Leda and Zeus and abducted by Theseus.
scenes.stakes: Tyndareus and Icarius lose their kingdom.

scenes.title: The suitors' oath
scenes.summary: Helen's many suitors gather. Ulysses proposes an oath to prevent quarrels, and Menelaus is chosen.
scenes.stakes: Tyndareus fears quarrels among the suitors.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains Aesculapius' power to raise the dead through Gorgon's blood.
The oath of Helen's suitors, which later drives the Trojan War.

analysis.text: The chapter is a genealogy linking gods and Spartan heroes, setting up the Trojan War through Helen's birth and the suitors' oath.
Apollodorus cites poets such as Stesichorus and Panyasis, showing how mythographers compiled variant traditions.

legacy.text: Hermes' invention of the lyre from a tortoise shell is told in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes and became a standard myth.
Aesculapius became the Greek god of medicine, and his serpent-entwined rod remains a medical symbol.

fun_facts.text: The text gives alternative versions, such as Helen being the daughter of Nemesis hatched from an egg.

language_notes.text: "To wit" is an archaic legal phrase meaning "that is to say," introducing the list of names.
The Islands of the Blest were the paradise where favored heroes lived after death, at the western edge of the world.
Kine is an old plural of "cow," meaning cattle.
A winnowing fan was a broad basket used to toss grain and separate chaff; here it serves as a cradle.
A plectrum is a small tool for plucking or striking the strings of a lyre.
Apollo was the god of prophecy, so he could identify the thief by divination without any tracks.
"Howbeit" is archaic for "however" or "nevertheless."
Divination by pebbles was a form of casting lots, where the pattern or choice of pebbles was read as an oracle.
"Son of the soil" means born from the earth itself, i.e. autochthonous, rather than from human parents.
A quoit is a heavy flat ring or disc thrown as a game; here it works like a discus.
"Involuntarily" means accidentally: Apollo killed Hyacinth by mistake, not by intent.
"Cohabited" means lived and slept with as a partner; "consorted" similarly means had intercourse.
The Gorgon is Medusa, killed by Perseus; her blood was thought to hold powers of both harm and healing.
Stesichorus, Panyasis and Melesagoras are earlier poets or writers whom the author cites as sources for variant myths.
"Smote" is the old past tense of smite, meaning struck hard. Zeus fears Aesculapius's skill at raising the dead would make humans less mortal.
The Cyclopes were smiths who made Zeus's thunderbolt. Apollo takes revenge on them because the thunderbolt killed his son Aesculapius.
A "thrall" is a slave or bondservant. Apollo's service is a punishment imposed by Zeus.
"To wit" is an archaic phrase meaning "that is to say" or "namely", introducing a list.
"Consorted" here means had sexual relations; "cohabited" repeats the idea for Tyndareus, explaining the twin paternity.
Theseus, the Athenian hero, abducted Helen when she was young and left her at Aphidnae in Attica.
"Wooers" means suitors, men seeking Helen's hand in marriage.
"Solicited" here means earnestly asked or urged, not sought a payment.

context_notes.text: The Pleiades were seven sisters who became the star cluster of that name. Atlas is the Titan who holds up the sky.
Poseidon is the god of the sea, who also fathered many heroes and monsters.
Pylus was a city in the southwestern Peloponnese, later associated with the king Nestor.
As herald, Hermes carries messages for Zeus and guides souls to the underworld, which fits his role as divine messenger.
Lynceus's keen sight became proverbial; the later phrase "lynx-eyed" echoes his name.
The Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux, twin heroes who abducted Leucippus's daughters.
Chiron was a wise centaur who tutored many heroes, including Achilles, in medicine and other skills.
Aesculapius became the Greek god of medicine; raising the dead later brought punishment from Zeus in the tradition.
Aesculapius was Apollo's son, a physician so skilled that he could restore the dead to life.
Admetus was a king of Pherae in Thessaly; Apollo's service to him is a well-known episode.
Hercules was avenging a debt to Tyndareus's family after Hippocoon's sons had wronged him.
This oath binds the suitors to defend Helen's husband, and later explains why the Greek kings join the Trojan War.

literary_notes.text: The newborn thief shows cunning by putting shoes on the cattle, a clever reversal of normal tracking.
Maia's showing the baby in swaddling-bands offers innocence as an alibi, contrasting with the elaborate theft just performed.
The exchange of pipe for divination shows Hermes gaining authority through trade and cleverness, marking his role as a god of exchange.
The raven's black color is explained as Apollo's curse, a myth giving an origin for a natural feature.
The blood from the left side harms and from the right side saves, balancing destruction against healing.
The compiler offers a rival version with "some say", presenting myth as varying tradition rather than a single authoritative story.
The long list of suitors and fathers gives a sense of Helen's fame and foreshadows the great army gathered for Troy.
Ulysses is shown as shrewd: he trades his clever plan for help in winning Penelope.
